dimensions.note: The pve-token secret travels only as an `Authorization: PVEAPIToken=...` request header. It is never logged, never written to a resource, and never interpolated into a detail string — the malformed-secret branch returns a fixed sentence and deliberately does not echo its input, which is the branch most likely to be tempted into quoting what it rejected. parsePveToken splits `user@realm!tokenid=<secret>` and returns ONLY the two identifiers before the `=`; the secret half is never returned, so the userid placed in the URL and the userid/tokenid placed in two detail strings are addresses, not credential material. The `unreachable` branch stringifies the fetch cause, which can carry the URL but not a header value. Mechanical check: no field of CredentialSchema or AuditSchema is secret-bearing, unchanged by this revision.

This revision adds no logging. All logging remains in the audit method — one structured line per credential plus a completion line — and the new probe returns a ProbeResult rather than emitting anything itself, so it cannot introduce a secret onto a log path.

probePveToken never throws. Every outcome maps to a distinct status with the cause in `detail`: malformed secret (authFailed, before any network call), network throw (unreachable), 401 (authFailed), 403 (noExpiry), other non-2xx (unreachable, carrying the code), non-JSON 2xx body (unreachable), tokenid absent from the map (authFailed), non-numeric or zero expire (noExpiry). Because it cannot throw, one unreachable Proxmox endpoint cannot abort the audit of every other credential — the partial-audit-reporting-success failure this model exists to prevent.

40 tests, 11 new for this revision, all against mocked fetch with no live calls. Covered: the parse and five malformed-input shapes; the exact URL including percent-encoding of the `@` in the userid; expire:0; a tokenid missing from the map; 401 vs 403; a network throw; a malformed secret short-circuiting BEFORE any request (asserted by a flag on the stub, not merely by the returned status); trailing-slash base URL; a non-JSON 2xx body; and a non-numeric expire. The last two were added during this review — I had guarded both in code without exercising them, which is exactly the gap this dimension is for. `probeFor covers every declared probe kind` still guards against adding a kind with no probe behind it.

Read-only by construction: the new probe is a single GET, and the model still exposes no method that can create, rotate or revoke anything. Verified empirically against a live cluster rather than by reading the code — the monitoring token this probe is built for returns 403 to both `POST /access/users/{u}/token/{new}` and `POST /nodes/{n}/qemu/{id}/status/stop`. Re-running is inherently safe; a partially completed run leaves no external state.

Endpoint choice is the substance of this change and was verified against a live cluster, not inferred. `GET /access/users/{userid}/token/{tokenid}` returns 403 to a PVEAuditor token because it requires User.Modify — permission to create and delete that user's tokens. `GET /access/users/{userid}` returns 200 with a `tokens` map embedding the same `expire`, needing only Sys.Audit. The 401-vs-403 split was observed, not assumed: a refused token gives 401, a valid token lacking Sys.Audit gives 403. `expire: 0` as Proxmox's encoding for 'never' was confirmed against a real never-expiring token. Response fields are read with typeof guards; no pagination applies to a single user record; AbortSignal.timeout bounds the request.

No file handles, sockets or temp files. One fetch, with AbortSignal.timeout(globalArgs.timeoutMs) as on every other probe. The response body is consumed exactly once, inside a try, on the only path that reads it. The model creates no external resources, so there is nothing to track for cleanup.

Re-checked across every shipped file for this revision. The README example uses `pve-token/builder@pve!provisioner` and `https://pve.example.com`; the code default is `https://pve.example.invalid`; tests use `pve.example.com` and `monitor@pve!expiry` with an all-zero placeholder uuid. Grep for internal hostnames, the internal domain, RFC1918 literals and the tailnet suffix across extensions/ and README.md returns nothing. The default host is intentionally a reserved-TLD name that cannot resolve, so a missing override fails as `unreachable` rather than probing an unintended real host.

PROBE_KINDS is extended in place, so `kind` stays an exact z.enum and CredentialSchema.kind narrows with it. pveBaseUrl is z.string().url() with a default — validated as a URL rather than accepted as free text. No .passthrough() anywhere; CredentialSchema and AuditSchema keep their exact declared shape, so CEL expression validation over resource attributes continues to resolve.
Unchanged. Both resources remain lifetime 'infinite' with garbageCollection 30. This revision adds no resource spec, so nothing accumulates that was not already bounded.

Not applicable by design, and deliberately so: the model has a single `audit` method and no create/update/delete surface. That absence is the safety argument for scheduling it unattended against production credentials, and this revision preserves it — the new kind adds a read, not a write.

preflight() is unchanged and still refuses the whole run on duplicate ids or ids that collide after normalisation. The new probe adds a per-credential fail-fast of its own: a secret not in `user@realm!tokenid=<secret>` form returns before any network call, which a test asserts by flagging the stub rather than by inspecting only the status.

resourceNameFor is unchanged and normalises a pve-token id such as `pve-token/terraform@pve!tf-proxmox-docker` to `pve-token-terraform-pve-tf-proxmox-docker`. The `@` and `!` characters common in Proxmox ids all fall into the same replacement class, which makes post-normalisation collisions MORE likely for this kind than for the others — two ids differing only in those characters would map to one instance and silently overwrite. That is precisely the case preflight() already refuses the run over, so the risk is detected rather than latent, and it is covered by an existing test.

The model reads no data artifacts — it writes resources and returns a summary. `data.latest()` appears only in the consuming workflow, not in this code, so nothing here can be broken by an instance-name change or a missing prior instance.

This revision ADDS the upgrades array the model had never carried. Declared as a no-op `upgradeAttributes: (old) => old` because the change is purely additive: no stored attribute changes shape, and existing jwt / github-pat / gitlab-pat entries keep their behaviour exactly. Declaring it matters even so — without an entry, existing instances pin to the version they were created at and would never pick up the new probe kind. pveBaseUrl carries a default, so a model that does not set it still validates.
